findings.title: Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The background cleanup loop's ticker was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This makes every cleanup job (temp files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, annotations, user invites, short URLs, query history) run ten times more often in production, which is a significant and unrelated change in DB/IO load for all Grafana installations. Note also that `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running cleanup cycle will be immediately followed by another one. This looks like a leftover from local reproduction of the deadlock and should be reverted to 10 minutes (or made configurable) before merge.

findings.title: Leftover debug logging at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: `CleanAnnotations` and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` log six messages per batch via `r.log.Error(...)` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579), e.g. `r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, ...)`. These are informational/debug messages, not errors: they will fire on every cleanup batch for every healthy installation, polluting error logs and triggering alerting on error-level log volume. They also serialize the entire ID slice into the log line — with the documented batch sizes (e.g. the 32767 used in the new test) each line can be hundreds of kilobytes. In addition, the `"err", err` field is always nil at these call sites because the error path returns earlier. These calls should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID slice.

findings.title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for SQLite
findings.body: In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite path builds the IN-list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over all IDs. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the list is O(n^2) in bytes copied. With a batch size such as the 32767 exercised by the new test, this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch and allocates 32k intermediate strings, for every delete batch of the cleanup job. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

findings.title: Placeholder-limit workaround only covers SQLite and keys off config instead of actual ID count
findings.body: `deleteByIDs` only avoids bind parameters when `r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. MySQL and Postgres have their own hard limit of 65535 placeholders per statement, so an operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will get every cleanup batch failing with a driver error on those backends. The condition also tests the configured batch size rather than `len(ids)`, which couples correctness of the statement to a config value instead of the data actually being deleted. Consider branching on `len(ids)` and applying a placeholder cap for all dialects (or chunking the delete).

findings.title: Per-subtest data cleanup is registered after the assertions that can abort the subtest
findings.body: `createTestAnnotations` is called, then `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` run (both use `require`, which calls `FailNow`), and only afterwards is `t.Cleanup` registered to delete from `annotation`/`annotation_tag`. If either pre-condition assertion fails, the subtest aborts before the cleanup is registered, so the inserted rows stay in the shared `fakeSQL` database and every subsequent subtest (which now assumes an empty table and asserts exact counts) fails with confusing cascading errors. Register the `t.Cleanup` immediately after creating the annotations, before asserting.
